Q: How to implement the deterministic version of Algorithm 1 from my 3-SAT paper in Python? A:

Use the lowest-index unsatisfied clause and lowest-index variable for deterministic tie-breaking. For performance, maintain each clause’s satisfied state and total weighted penalty, then update only clauses in var_to_clauses after a flip instead of rescanning the whole formula.

Also check the paper’s exact definition of “stagnation”: the current prototype increases λ after every flip, which may differ from Algorithm 1. Comparing the optimized version against the slow implementation on small formulas is a good way to verify correctness.

Q: How do I prevent violation of UNIQUE KEY constraint caused by lots of inserts coming from 2 sessions A:

The root cause is in this code section:

insert #Data with (tablockx) (TransactionCode)
    select CHECKSUM(newid()) % 10000
    from GENERATE_SERIES(1, 100);

That CHECKSUM(newid()) % 10000 expression can have only up to 10,000 random numbers, meaning the number will be wrapped around at the 10,001st time.

Since there are 100 rows to be inserted or updated each time, after doing that 100 times, the TransactionCode will inevitably collide with one that already exists in the stored data.

Solution

It would be a better choice to use a sequence instead to avoid the collision:

CREATE    SEQUENCE dbo.TransactionCodeSeq
AS        INT
START     WITH 1
INCREMENT BY 1;

GO

-- ...

INSERT #Data (TransactionCode)
SELECT NEXT VALUE
FOR    dbo.TransactionCodeSeq
FROM   GENERATE_SERIES(1, 100);

By the way, #Data is a temp table, each session gets its own instance of it even when having the same name.

There's really no point to use with (tablockx) in the original code to lock it exclusively.

Serial, not random

Please note that the numbers generated from a SEQUENCE are always serial, starting from 1. It's not a random number generator.

SQL Server comes with a floating point generator RAND() which return values range from 0.0 to 1.0. You can use the expression FLOOR(RAND() * 2147483647) to get a random integer value, where 2147483647 is the maximum for INT type. However, this does not guarantee the uniqueness of the result. For the purpose as a unique column like TransactionCode, using a sequence is the safest bet.

References

  • CREATE SEQUENCE (Transact-SQL) - SQL Server | Microsoft Learn
  • RAND (Transact-SQL) - SQL Server | Microsoft Learn

Q: Multithreaded Pygame A:

According to the SDL FAQ (Pygame wraps SDL), you can't rely on graphics being accessible from multiple threads. You would have to transfer all your drawing to the main thread. You can still have threads running other logic.

Note that they say "main thread". It is not enough in general to use a lock. You could e.g. set up a queue with jobs to run on the main thread, and feed that queue, as long as the jobs in there can run safely in a different thread (e.g. are protected with a lock around the state they need to know what to draw).
